plot_extraction.response_text:
A traveler with a ruined appetite visits a Bohemian health resort run by Professor Haimberger. The professor offers him a menu of revolting dishes, locks him in his room, and refuses him ordinary food. As the traveler goes without eating, books about shipwrecks and starvation intensify his hunger. After sixty hours, he becomes willing to eat even the menu’s grotesque offerings. The professor then serves him chicken, followed by steak, potatoes, bread, and coffee, which he devours with delight, proving that his appetite has returned.

Haimberger explains that he developed this cure after surviving a shipwreck. During the voyage, passengers had lost interest in the ship’s monotonous meals, but severe rationing after the wreck made them ravenous enough to relish raw ham and even softened sailor boots. Once rescued, however, they resumed regular eating and soon lost their appetites again.

From this experience, Haimberger concludes that people should eat only when genuinely hungry and should skip meals whenever food ceases to taste satisfying. He argues that conventional health resorts secretly achieve results through restricted diets rather than water, baths, or other advertised treatments. He advises the traveler to return to his former habit of one and a half meals a day, since adding an unnecessary luncheon caused his condition, and recommends brief fasting as a remedy for minor illnesses.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story adopts the manner of a comic travel memoir that gradually turns into a satirical case study. Its first-person narrator presents himself as an experienced, sociable traveller, moving easily from geographical description and personal reminiscence to anecdote, dialogue and argumentative reflection. He is observant but deliberately digressive: the opening discussion of a Bohemian health resort wanders into an enthusiastic account of a hidden Viennese beer cellar before returning, with the self-conscious remark that the episode is “all incidental,” to the ostensible subject. Such detours create an informal, conversational impression while also establishing the narrator’s comic personality.

The prevailing tone is dry, genial and irreverent. Serious institutions—medicine, health tourism, dietary doctrine and respectable social custom—are treated with amused suspicion. The humour often depends on stating absurdities with complete confidence. Austria is described as an empire made up of health resorts that “distributes health to the whole world,” while its supposedly medicinal waters are exported because the natives prefer beer. The appetite clinic’s grotesque menu is likewise administered with professional solemnity, allowing the contrast between the doctor’s composure and the patient’s horror to generate comedy. Hyperbole is central: trains are phenomenally slow, a biscuit could be fired to a nearby resort with a twelve-inch gun, and disagreeable food is described as fit to “gag a cannibal.” These exaggerations remain anchored in recognisable frustrations, so the absurdity sharpens rather than replaces the social satire.

The diction combines cultivated, occasionally old-fashioned prose with colloquial American phrasing. Elevated words such as “outlanders,” “domicile,” “repose,” “paucity” and “surreptitious” sit beside idioms such as “hand-spring,” “buzzard-fare,” “right along,” “set them up” and “I can’t spare my mouth.” This mixture allows the narrator to sound both literate and plain-speaking. Mock-technical language is especially important. Terms including “Appetite Anstallt,” “robust treatment,” “the corrective” and “Nature’s Appetite-Cure” imitate the authority of medical discourse, while grotesque images expose the simplicity concealed beneath it. Concrete food vocabulary recurs obsessively, ranging from Vienna bread and coffee to raw ham, sailor-boots, butterflies and filtered sewage. Accumulated lists of dishes give the prose sensory force and turn appetite itself into a structural motif.

The syntax is highly varied. Descriptive and expository passages favour long, cumulative sentences joined by semicolons, dashes and repeated clauses. These sentences mimic spontaneous speech, permitting qualifications, jokes and side comments to interrupt the main line of thought. Short sentences then provide comic emphasis: “It was refused me,” “It is all so handy,” or “They were human beings.” Dashes frequently control timing, postponing a conclusion or introducing a sharper afterthought. Colons are used for catalogues and mock demonstrations, while repetition supplies rhetorical momentum. The doctor’s insistence that the cure “never failed—never” and his repeated commands not to eat create both persuasive force and farce.

Dialogue dominates much of the narrative and is constructed as brisk verbal sparring. The narrator plays the sceptical, indignant patient, while Professor Haimberger answers with unwavering literalness. Their exchanges often proceed through short questions, reversals and delayed explanations. A proposition that initially sounds insane is slowly revealed as practical, whereas respectable conventional wisdom comes to appear foolish. The doctor’s voice is authoritative, blunt and paradoxical; he uses categorical statements, analogies and provocative generalisations about human stupidity. The narrator’s voice is more reactive and figurative, full of mock outrage, but he is willing to concede defeat when experience proves the system effective. This interplay keeps an extended argument lively and prevents the didactic material from becoming a conventional lecture.

Structurally, the story has two distinct movements. The first is an experiential comic narrative: arrival at the clinic, confrontation with the menu, confinement, mounting hunger and eventual surrender. Its tension is produced by deprivation and escalation. As the hours without food accumulate, the patient’s standards steadily collapse until the once-repellent dishes become desirable. The climax arrives with the deliberately nonsensical “soft-boiled spring chicken—in the egg,” followed by an enormous ordinary meal. The second movement explains the theory behind the cure through the doctor’s shipwreck story and a long Socratic conversation. This section is more discursive, but it retains narrative energy through miniature examples, grotesque catalogues and argumentative reversals. The final assertion that the narrator has personally tested the method gives the piece the form of humorous testimony.

The pacing alternates between leisurely digression and rapid escalation. Scenic descriptions of Vienna and the mountain resort are spacious and appreciative, with visual phrases such as “green glades and valleys” and “tumbled hills clothed with forests.” By contrast, the period of confinement is compressed through counted hours and repeated attempts to order food. The second half slows to examine the cure’s principles, though comic images—patients eating eggs, butterflies and rose leaves or walking off their medicinal water—continually refresh the exposition. Enumeration is a major pacing device: lists initially overwhelm the reader, then culminate in a succinct punch line or blunt conclusion.

The narrator’s reliability is playfully unstable. He reports places, meals and experiences with documentary specificity, yet embellishes them so extravagantly that factual truth becomes secondary to comic truth. He is also the target of the satire as well as its vehicle. His attachment to routine, refined food and inherited assumptions makes him one of the foolish patients he describes. The eventual conversion does not erase his vanity; instead, it permits him to join the doctor in judging humanity. This self-implicating quality softens the satire and preserves the narrator’s amiability.

Thematically, the story attacks unexamined habit, fashionable medicine and dependence on authority. Its central paradox is that deprivation restores pleasure: hunger, rather than delicacy or elaborate treatment, makes food nourishing and desirable. The appetite cure also serves as a broader allegory of common sense obscured by convention. Human beings ignore direct bodily evidence, submit to schedules and superstitions, and then pay experts to disguise simple remedies as complicated regimens. Yet the satire is not entirely anti-medical. Professor Haimberger succeeds because he understands psychology, manipulates expectation and forces patients to discover a truth through experience. The resulting style blends travel writing, tall tale, mock-scientific discourse, social criticism and practical sermon, all unified by deadpan delivery, vivid exaggeration and a strong instinct for the comic reversal.

generation.response_text:
### Professor Haimberger’s Establishment

Austria, as nearly as I could determine during three months of conscientious travel, is a federation of health resorts connected by trains which move slowly enough to give the invalid ample opportunity to die before reaching any of them.

Every valley has its spring, every spring has its analysis, and every analysis proves that the water contains precisely those minerals which mankind has been lacking since the Flood. The native, being familiar with these waters from infancy, drinks beer. He is not ungrateful; he merely believes that the mineral water ought to be preserved for strangers who have paid for railway tickets.

I was bound for Grünwald, in Bohemia, where Professor Alois Haimberger maintained an establishment for the treatment of impaired appetite. My own appetite had been failing for six months. It had not failed noisily or with theatrical effect; it had simply withdrawn from public life. At breakfast it appeared in a perfunctory manner, glanced at the rolls, and retired. At luncheon it sent regrets. At dinner it sometimes consented to be represented by a small fish and a glass of wine, but the old enthusiasm was gone.

This was serious, because eating had always been one of my dependable gifts. I could not sing, paint, run for office, or understand a railway timetable, but I could eat with judgment, courage and continuity. When that faculty deserted me I felt as a banker must feel upon discovering that he has lost his arithmetic.

A physician in Vienna recommended Professor Haimberger.

“He has a remarkable clinic,” the physician said. “His methods are severe, but his results are permanent.”

“What are his methods?”

“He will explain them.”

A doctor who refuses to explain another doctor’s methods is either loyal or alarmed. In either case the patient is expected to furnish the courage.

I remained in Vienna two days before taking the train to Grünwald, and there encountered a subterranean beer cellar which deserves a chapter, a monument and an annual procession. It lay beneath an unimportant street and was entered by a door so narrow that a prosperous magistrate could pass through it only after making a legal concession. A stair descended into coolness and golden light. At the bottom were long halls with vaulted roofs, copper lamps, oak tables, white-aproned waiters and citizens of such settled contentment that one felt the Austro-Hungarian Empire could never collapse while they remained seated.

The beer arrived in stone mugs, cold and grave and crowned with foam. With it came brown bread, white radishes, smoked sausage, pickled onions, cheese perfumed like a political scandal, and a mustard capable of restoring consciousness to a bronze statue. A military band played somewhere beyond a stone arch. Nobody hurried. Nobody demanded improvement. Men lifted their mugs, contemplated them, drank, and replaced them with the calm of priests performing an old rite.

I mention this cellar because I visited it three times in two days and ate almost nothing. The fact disturbed me more than the medical diagnosis had done. In former years I could have disposed of that sausage with one hand while signalling for reinforcements with the other. Now I nibbled a radish and became fatigued.

The cellar is incidental, but the best portions of travel are usually incidental; the official objects are churches, galleries and palaces, whereas the things remembered are a waiter’s whiskers, a dog asleep in a doorway, and the precise taste of beer in a room thirty feet below the taxes.

On the third morning I took the train to Grünwald.

It travelled through green valleys, around forested hills, across bright rivers, and occasionally forward. At each station it rested with the dignity of a public institution. Peasants arrived, embraced relatives, loaded baskets, unloaded baskets, argued with officials, drank coffee, changed their minds, and departed again, while our locomotive stood breathing heavily as if it had accomplished all this itself.

Grünwald occupied a fold in the mountains. There were white hotels, red roofs, shaded promenades, orchestras in pavilions, shops selling carved bears, and solemn people walking about with graduated drinking glasses. At six in the morning the patients drank water. At seven they walked it off. At eight they ate an extensive breakfast to recover from the walk. At ten they drank more water, and at noon they ate again to prevent the water from weakening them. The arrangement was scientific and had the additional merit of supporting every hotel in town.

Professor Haimberger’s establishment stood above the village among dark fir trees. It was a square stone building with green shutters, broad balconies and the hygienic expression of a prison that has recently been whitewashed.

The professor received me in a large bare office. He was short, broad, bald, bearded and composed. His spectacles were circular, his coat was black, and his hands were clean enough to perform an operation upon the archduke’s conscience.

“You have no appetite,” he said.

“Very little.”

“How many meals?”

“Ordinarily?”

“Nothing is ordinary. How many?”

“Breakfast, luncheon and dinner.”

“Before the illness?”

“For most of my life, breakfast and dinner. Sometimes a bite at midday.”

“And when did you begin regular luncheon?”

“About seven months ago.”

“And the appetite failed six months ago.”

“That is approximately true.”

“It is exactly true. You have been eating one meal more than you required, and now you complain because you do not desire four.”

“Three.”

“You count by plates. I count by burdens.”

He tapped a bell. An attendant entered and brought a printed card. The professor handed it to me.

“There is your diet.”

The card was headed, in Gothic letters, **HAIMBERGER’S RESTORATIVE BILL OF FARE—FIRST DEGREE**. Beneath this announcement appeared the following:

Boiled carp skin with lukewarm vinegar.  
Cold mutton fat with anise.  
Stewed cucumber ends.  
Pickled crow.  
Calf gristle in sour milk.  
Turnip pudding with cod-liver sauce.  
Roasted beetles, when obtainable.  
Compote of prunes and garlic.  
Gray bread soaked in cabbage water.

I read it twice, because a man naturally hopes that horror will improve upon closer acquaintance.

“Which of these am I expected to eat?” I asked.

“Whichever you prefer.”

“I prefer an omelet.”

“It is not there.”

“A chop?”

“Not there.”

“Chicken?”

“Later, perhaps.”

“Professor, that list would embarrass a hyena.”

He took the card and examined it with professional interest.

“The beetles are seasonal,” he said. “You need not depend upon them.”

“I will not depend upon any portion of it. Bring me coffee and rolls.”

“No.”

“Then tea and toast.”

“No.”

“A biscuit.”

“No.”

“An apple.”

“No.”

“What am I to have?”

“Your choice from the card.”

“I choose starvation.”

“Excellent,” he said. “That is our most successful dish.”

He conducted me upstairs to a pleasant room overlooking the valley. It contained a bed, an armchair, a writing desk, a washstand, and a locked cabinet whose key he removed. There was no bell rope. The windows opened upon a drop of thirty feet.

“You will remain here,” he said. “An attendant will come at intervals. You may order anything on the card.”

“And if I order beefsteak?”

“It will not come.”

“If I leave?”

“The door is locked.”

“This is not medicine. It is abduction.”

“Abduction costs more. This is included in the fee.”

He bowed and left.

For the first six hours I was amused. I wrote letters. I described the professor’s menu to friends and improved it with imaginary delicacies—fried umbrella handles, boiled piano keys, and old gloves stuffed with lampblack. At noon an attendant entered carrying a covered dish.

“What is that?”

“Calf gristle, sir.”

“Take it away.”

“It is nourishing.”

“So is the attendant, presumably, but I do not intend to eat him.”

At four I requested coffee. It was refused. At six I asked for bread. It was refused. At seven I demanded to see the professor. He came promptly, which is more than ordinary doctors do when they intend to be useful.

“This has gone far enough,” I said.

“It has scarcely begun.”

“I have eaten nothing since yesterday evening.”

“Good.”

“It is not good. I am weak.”

“You walked across the room when I entered.”

“Must I crawl before I qualify for dinner?”

“You must become hungry.”

“I am hungry now.”

He placed the menu before me.

I looked at it and handed it back.

“You are offended,” he said. “You are not hungry.”

“I know my own stomach.”

“No man does. If men knew their stomachs, half the physicians and nearly all the pastry cooks would be unemployed.”

“I can eat ordinary food.”

“You can swallow it. That is not the same thing.”

He left me.

Night came. The lights of Grünwald glittered below. From the hotel terraces floated music, laughter and, unless my nerves deceived me, the clatter of knives and forks. The mountain air carried fragrances uphill: roasted meat, coffee, tobacco, warm bread. It seemed unreasonable that odors should be allowed to travel freely while I was detained.

I went to bed early and dreamed of the Viennese cellar. In the dream the stone mugs were filled with gravy, and the sausages marched past me in military formation while a waiter demanded my passport. I awoke at two and found myself chewing the corner of the sheet.

In the morning the attendant brought the card.

“Breakfast?” he inquired.

“Coffee, eggs, rolls, honey.”

He indicated the printed list.

“Then nothing.”

He bowed. I disliked the grace with which he accepted my decision.

On the writing desk I discovered several books selected, no doubt, for the moral uplift of patients. There was an account of Arctic exploration, the memoirs of a missionary in a desert, two narratives of shipwreck, and a volume entitled *Notable Famines of Central Europe*. Professor Haimberger’s library possessed unity.

I began the Arctic book. By page thirty the explorers had eaten their dogs. By page fifty they had boiled harness straps. At page seventy-one a lieutenant spent four paragraphs describing half a candle. His language was indecently appetizing. The wax had been rancid, mixed with lint and gnawed by mice, yet he remembered it after twenty years with tears of gratitude.

I threw the book aside and opened a shipwreck narrative. The survivors had lived for eleven days on rainwater, two oranges and the leather cover of a hymnbook. One man had concealed a dried pea. When it was discovered, the entire company discussed whether he ought to be hanged before or after the pea was divided.

I closed that book also.

At noon the attendant appeared with pickled crow.

The bird lay upon a platter, dark, narrow and disapproving. Its legs pointed upward. A wreath of parsley had been placed around it, which seemed less an ornament than an apology.

“Take it away,” I said, but not immediately.

The attendant noticed the interval. Attendants in clinics are trained to detect weakness.

“Very tender, sir.”

“Go.”

“With mustard—”

“Go!”

He went, taking the crow, and I followed it with my eyes.

That afternoon I tried to work, but my thoughts would not remain on any subject that could not be buttered. I began a letter: “My dear Charles, the political condition of Europe—” and then found I had written “Europe should be browned evenly and served with potatoes.”

At thirty hours I could have eaten the gray bread if the cabbage water had been omitted. At thirty-six hours I was prepared to negotiate about the water. At forty hours the stewed cucumber ends lost their criminal aspect. At forty-five I considered the mutton fat and decided that anise, though objectionable in principle, might possess unsuspected virtues.

The professor called.

“Well?” he said.

“I could eat something.”

He gave me the card.

I examined it with attention. It had ceased to be a document of outrage and had become a collection of opportunities.

“The turnip pudding,” I said cautiously. “How much cod-liver sauce?”

“Enough.”

“That is not a measurement.”

“It is the correct measurement.”

“Could the sauce be brought separately?”

“No.”

“Then perhaps the gristle.”

“With sour milk.”

“Yes, I can read.”

“You do not sound hungry.”

“I am not required to sound it. Hunger is not an opera.”

He withdrew the card.

“No food yet.”

I expressed myself in terms unsuitable for a health resort. He listened without resentment.

“Anger is often the last defense of habit,” he said.

“It may also be the first defense of a patient who intends to throw his doctor off a balcony.”

“You are becoming vigorous.”

At forty-eight hours I reread the story of the hymnbook cover and envied the survivors. At fifty-two I drank water and found it had flavor. At fifty-five I caught myself considering whether the leather binding of *Notable Famines* belonged to the library or could be charged to my account.

At fifty-eight hours the attendant brought the prunes and garlic. Steam rose from the bowl. The odor was violent, but it was an odor associated with food, and this distinction now outweighed all others.

“I will take it,” I said.

He shook his head. “The professor must decide.”

“You offered it.”

“I exhibited it.”

“You fiend!”

“It is part of the examination.”

I lunged for the bowl; he retreated with professional agility and locked the door behind him.

At sixty hours Professor Haimberger entered.

He carried the menu.

“What will you eat?”

“All of it.”

“Choose one dish.”

“The crow.”

“With pleasure.”

“And the gristle.”

“One dish.”

“The mutton fat, then. No—the pudding. Bring the pudding. Bring anything that has once been within speaking distance of a kitchen.”

“Would you eat an egg?”

“Shell and all.”

“A young chicken?”

“Feathers optional.”

“Potatoes?”

“Raw, cooked, stolen or inherited.”

He considered me solemnly. “The cure has taken effect.”

He clapped his hands. Two attendants entered carrying a table laid with a white cloth, silver, china and a covered platter. Another followed with bread, butter and coffee. A fourth brought vegetables.

The professor lifted the cover.

There lay a roasted chicken, brown, crisp-skinned and surrounded by its own golden juices.

I looked at him. I looked at the chicken. Emotion obstructed my speech.

“You said—” I began.

“I said you might have chicken later.”

“This is later.”

“It usually is.”

I sat down. He carved.

The first mouthful was a revelation. I had eaten chickens in Paris, Vienna, New York, Rome and in certain American towns where the bird is cooked until it can be used as building material; but no chicken had ever tasted like this one. It possessed tenderness, fragrance, dignity and moral worth. I could have made a speech over it, but I had no spare mouth.

After the chicken came a thick beefsteak, charred outside and red within. There were potatoes browned in butter, peas, hot bread, a salad, cheese and coffee. I ate everything. I did not nibble, inspect, compare or criticize. I ate as an honest furnace receives coal.

The professor watched without surprise.

“More steak?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“More potatoes?”

“Yes.”

“Bread?”

“Yes.”

“Coffee?”

“Yes.”

“Pickled crow?”

“No.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“I am cured,” I said, “not insane.”

When the meal ended I leaned back with the peace of a man who has regained both his appetite and his religion.

“Professor,” I said, “your method is barbarous, unlawful, insulting and magnificent. Where did you discover it?”

“In the Indian Ocean.”

“I had not supposed Bohemian medicine travelled so far.”

“It travelled by accident. I was shipwrecked.”

He drew up a chair.

“Many years ago,” he said, “I sailed from Bombay upon a passenger steamer. We had been at sea three weeks when everyone began complaining of the food. It was good food—meat, fish, soup, vegetables, pudding—but it returned too regularly. At eight came breakfast, at one luncheon, at seven dinner. Between these, tea. The passengers ate because bells rang. They had no appetite, so they blamed the cook.

“One lady said the eggs had no character. A colonel declared the mutton melancholy. A merchant from Glasgow examined every potato as if it had applied for credit. We demanded sauces, relishes, curries, fresh fruit, new breads. The captain changed the menu. The complaints increased.

“Then the ship struck a reef at night. We took to the boats. There were thirty-one people in mine, with water, some raw ham, a tin of biscuits and no cook to abuse.

“The first day the ladies would not touch the ham because it was uncooked. The colonel said salt meat inflamed his gout. The merchant disliked the biscuits. They were damp.

“The second day they ate the biscuits.

“The third day they ate the ham.

“The fourth day they searched the boat for crumbs of both.

“After that we rationed everything: a swallow of water, a shaving of meat. One passenger had stuffed two biscuits into his coat during the confusion. When they were discovered, he explained that he had saved them for his wife. He had no wife aboard. He had no wife anywhere. Hunger had married him.”

“What happened when the food was gone?” I asked.

“We found more food.”

“Where?”

The professor looked at his boots.

“No.”

“Yes. Sailors’ boots are excellent if boiled six hours.”

“They are leather.”

“That is why five hours is insufficient.”

“You ate boots?”

“We softened them in seawater and cut them into strips. The uppers were better than the soles. One must avoid nails. The colonel, who had condemned the melancholy mutton, asked for a second helping of heel.”

“And the ladies?”

“They chewed laces. Refinement survives many things, but not genuine hunger.”

“How long were you adrift?”

“Twelve days. A freighter rescued us. They brought soup, bread and coffee. We ate. We wept. We praised the cook. For two weeks no one criticized anything. Then regular meals resumed, appetite diminished, and one morning I heard the colonel complain that an egg was overdone.

“That egg created my establishment.”

I waited.

“Do you not understand?” he said. “The shipwreck did not damage our appetites. The ship had damaged them; the wreck restored them. We had eaten by the clock until food became labor. Deprivation made it pleasure again.”

“That is simple.”

“All important discoveries are simple after someone else has paid for the shipwreck.”

“But surely a civilized person cannot wait until he wishes to eat footwear.”

“He need not. He must merely wait until bread seems desirable.”

“You recommend fasting?”

“I recommend not eating when one is not hungry.”

“That sounds like fasting.”

“It sounds like common sense. Therefore society requires a foreign professor, a stone building and a substantial fee before it will consider the idea.”

He poured himself coffee.

“Observe the health resorts,” he continued. “At one place the patient drinks sulfur water. At another he bathes in mud. Elsewhere he is wrapped in wet sheets, struck with cold sprays, steamed, rubbed, rolled, electrified and made to walk uphill before breakfast. Each resort advertises a different miracle. Yet the successful ones have one rule in common.”

“What rule?”

“They restrict the table.”

I thought of Grünwald’s hotels and their extensive meals.

“Not here.”

“Those are hotels. They cure loneliness.”

“But the patients eat constantly.”

“Then they will return next year. That is good management.”

He explained that a fashionable clinic might attribute improvement to radium water, pine air, blue clay or a spring possessing seventeen unpronounceable salts; but behind the scenery there was generally a stern woman weighing bread. The water received the testimonial. The kitchen scale did the work.

“A patient drinks three glasses of disgusting water,” he said. “Then he walks six miles because the doctor orders exercise. At breakfast he receives one egg. By noon he is hungry. He eats plain soup and says the water has awakened his stomach. If I gave him the egg and omitted the mineral water, he would distrust me.”

“Because your treatment would look too easy.”

“Exactly. Humanity does not value a cure unless it stains the tongue, empties the purse or requires a railway journey.”

I objected that regular meals were one of the supports of civilization.

“So are regular taxes,” he said. “That does not prove the body wants them.”

“Families must dine at fixed hours.”

“Let the hungry members dine.”

“And the others?”

“Let them talk.”

“A host cannot ask guests whether their stomachs are ready.”

“Then he should not complain when they have no appetite.”

“What of children?”

“Children know. Adults corrupt them. A child runs all morning and comes home hungry. The mother gives him sweets at eleven, luncheon at one, cake at four, dinner at seven, and medicine at eight because he picked at dinner. Then she says he has inherited a delicate constitution from his father.”

“What if a person feels ill?”

“Do not feed him.”

“That is your answer to every question.”

“No. If he breaks his leg, set the leg. But do not serve him pudding merely because the bone is broken.”

He had developed the principle into what he called the Voluntary Interval. Whenever food ceased to give honest pleasure, the patient skipped the next meal. If appetite had not returned, he skipped another. Water was allowed. So were fresh air, repose and ill temper. The interval rarely lasted beyond a day, he said, because most civilized persons had never given hunger a fair chance.

“People fear missing luncheon,” he said, “as if luncheon were a train for heaven.”

“Is there no danger?”

“For the healthy? Less danger than in eating without need. A man feels a cold beginning. His tongue is coated; food tastes dull. What does he do? He eats a large dinner to keep up his strength. Then he sleeps badly and blames the cold. If he left dinner alone, the body could attend to its business without first unpacking roast beef.”

“You prescribe starvation for a cold?”

“I prescribe an evening without roast beef. Language is what frightens patients. Call it ‘starvation’ and they resist; call it ‘metabolic repose’ and they pay thirty crowns.”

I asked whether his grotesque bill of fare was necessary.

“Entirely.”

“Why not simply refuse food?”

“Because then the patient thinks he is hungry from the first hour. The menu supplies a test. So long as he rejects the dishes, his hunger is imaginary. When he seriously desires pickled crow, I know he is ready for chicken.”

“Do you actually cook the crow?”

“We have cooked one crow for eleven years.”

“The same bird?”

“It is economical and commands respect.”

“And the beetles?”

“Wooden.”

“The gristle?”

“Rubber.”

“The prunes and garlic?”

“Genuine. The staff eats them.”

I felt injured.

“You tormented me with theatrical properties.”

“Medicine has always used theatrical properties. Mine are cheaper than marble baths.”

He then returned to my own history. For years, he said, I had lived well upon breakfast and dinner, with perhaps a small midday morsel when travel or sociability required it. Then some respectable acquaintance had persuaded me that luncheon was essential. I had inserted it between two sufficient meals. The new meal had not created new hunger; it had merely divided the old hunger into three feeble obligations.

“You trained yourself not to be hungry,” he said. “Then you travelled to Bohemia to learn hunger.”

“At considerable expense.”

“You would not respect the lesson otherwise.”

“What am I to do when I leave?”

“Return to your former habit. Eat breakfast if you want it. Eat dinner when you want it. At midday, ask your stomach, not your watch.”

“And if the stomach says nothing?”

“Do nothing.”

“That will be difficult in company.”

“Common sense always is. Folly has fixed hours and printed invitations.”

I remained at the establishment three more days. The professor fed me generously, but never until I asked with sincerity. Once, at noon, I requested luncheon from habit. He offered the menu. I withdrew the request. At four the smell of bread from the kitchen became eloquent, and he gave me bread, butter and cheese. I ate them with more pleasure than I had taken in elaborate banquets during the preceding year.

On my last morning I walked down to Grünwald. The orchestra was playing. Patients moved solemnly along the promenade, carrying glasses of mineral water which smelled like hot coins. One pale gentleman pinched his nose, swallowed his dose and immediately rewarded himself with a pastry. A stout lady drank two glasses, complained of fullness, and entered a restaurant to settle her nerves.

The whole machinery of fashionable health was in motion: springs bubbling, attendants measuring, bands performing, doctors consulting, cooks preparing, invalids eating to recover from remedies and taking remedies to recover from eating.

I do not say the waters were useless. They gave people something to believe in, and belief is often strengthening—particularly to the hotel proprietor. But I had learned to distrust any medicine whose principal ingredient could be replaced by patience.

Since then I have followed Haimberger’s rule, though not with saintly consistency. When food loses its invitation, I decline it. When a minor fever or cold appears, I allow a meal or two to pass without ceremony. Appetite returns like an offended friend who only wished to be missed.

I have recommended the method to others. They rarely accept it. One man told me he could not skip dinner because his physician had ordered regular nourishment. Another said fasting made him hungry, and therefore could not be wholesome. A third listened carefully, agreed with every word, and went directly to luncheon.

This is natural. People prefer a cure that requires them to swallow something. Abstaining seems inadequate; it leaves no bottle to display and no directions to misunderstand.

As for Professor Haimberger, his establishment prospered. He eventually enlarged it, installed a marble fountain and published an analysis of the local spring. The water, he confided to me, was ordinary mountain water; but patients demanded a mineral, so he added a Latin name and advised them to walk two miles before drinking it.

“Does the water cure them?” I asked on a later visit.

“No,” he said. “The walk makes them hungry.”

“And what does the fee do?”

“It makes them obedient.”

That was many years ago. I can no longer recall the chemical name of his spring, the altitude of Grünwald, or the number of windows in the clinic. But I remember the roasted chicken. I remember the bread, the potatoes and the coffee. Above all, I remember the solemn moment when pickled crow appeared reasonable.

A man may doubt many doctrines after travelling widely, but not one which has brought him safely from crow to chicken.

### The Keeper of Lost Hours

Every morning at six, Elias Vale unlocked the door beneath the clock tower and swept yesterday’s minutes from the floor.

They gathered in the corners like silver dust. Some were bright and warm, the remains of laughter that had ended too quickly. Others were gray and heavy, shed by people who had waited for letters, doctors, trains, or apologies that never came. Elias collected them carefully in a copper pan and poured them into labeled glass jars.

MISSED CHANCES.

UNSPOKEN WORDS.

SLEEPLESS NIGHTS.

LAST GOODBYES.

The jars filled the walls of his workshop from floor to ceiling. When sunlight passed through them, the room shimmered with moments no one remembered losing.

Elias was the Keeper of Lost Hours, though few people in Bellwether knew such a position existed. To the town, he was merely the thin, quiet man who maintained the great clock in the square. They saw him climbing ladders, oiling gears, and adjusting the iron hands after storms. They did not see what happened below.

They did not see him repair cracked seconds with tweezers.

They did not hear forgotten songs humming inside sealed bottles.

They did not know that every clock lost a little time, and that all lost time had to go somewhere.

The rules of his work had been taught to him by his predecessor, Mistress Ansel, who had served for fifty-seven years before retiring to a cottage by the sea.

“Time is neither kind nor cruel,” she had told him. “It is only obedient. The danger begins when people ask it to turn around.”

The first rule was simple: no lost hour could be returned to the person who had lost it.

The second: no hour could be used twice.

The third: the Keeper must never open a black jar.

Elias had obeyed these rules for eighteen years.

Then, one autumn afternoon, a girl named Mara Quill knocked on his door.

The workshop door was hidden behind the clock tower’s western stairwell and had no sign. Ordinary townspeople passed it without noticing. Mara knocked three times, paused, then knocked twice more.

Elias froze over his workbench.

No one had used that signal since Mistress Ansel left.

He opened the door a fraction. A girl of perhaps sixteen stood outside. Her dark hair had been hacked short with an unsteady hand. Rain soaked the shoulders of her green coat, and she held a pocket watch against her chest.

“You’re the Keeper,” she said.

“I repair clocks.”

“You collect lost time.”

Elias glanced past her. The stairwell was empty. “Who told you that?”

“My mother.”

“Who is your mother?”

“Lena Quill.”

The name struck him like the sudden chime of a bell.

For a moment, the tower seemed to tilt.

Lena Quill had been dead for fifteen years.

Elias opened the door.

Mara stepped inside and stared at the shelves. The jars responded to her presence with faint whispers and sighs. Somewhere high above, a bottle of childhood summers glowed golden.

“My mother said there would be jars,” Mara murmured. “I thought she was joking.”

“When did she tell you about this place?”

“Last night.”

Elias looked at her.

“She’s dying,” Mara continued. “The doctor says she has two days. Maybe less. She talks strangely now. Sometimes to me, sometimes to people who aren’t there. Last night she said I should bring you this.”

She placed the pocket watch on his workbench.

Elias knew it before he touched it. The silver case bore a tiny engraving of a swallow in flight. He pressed the catch, and the lid opened.

The watch hands had stopped at 11:43.

Inside the lid were six words:

WHEN THE BELLS FAIL, COME HOME.

His own hands began to tremble.

“I gave this to her,” he said.

Mara’s eyes narrowed. “You knew my mother?”

“Yes.”

“How?”

Elias closed the watch. “A long time ago, we were friends.”

“That isn’t true.”

He met her gaze.

“She had friends,” Mara said. “She spoke about them. But when she said your name, she cried.”

Rain tapped at the narrow windows. In the silence, the shelves murmured.

“We were more than friends,” Elias admitted.

Mara took a step back, as though the room had shifted beneath her. She studied his face more carefully. Her anger faded, replaced by calculation.

“How old are you?” she asked.

“Forty-one.”

“My mother is forty-two.”

“Yes.”

“Then why did she never mention you?”

“Because I asked her not to.”

“That’s a terrible answer.”

“It was a terrible request.”

Mara snatched the watch from the table. “She wants to see you.”

Elias looked toward the clockwork overhead. Through the ceiling came the steady movement of gears: tooth meeting tooth, each second locked into the next.

“I can’t leave the tower.”

“You climb outside it every week.”

“I mean I cannot leave my duty.”

“She has two days.”

“The town has thousands of clocks. They spill minutes constantly. If I abandon the workshop—”

“My mother is dying.”

Elias said nothing.

Mara’s expression hardened. “I thought you might be a coward. I didn’t think you’d be proud of it.”

She turned and walked out.

The door slammed. Several jars flickered, and one labeled WORDS REGRETTED gave a soft, bitter laugh.

Elias returned to his bench, but his hands were useless. He bent the same second three times. He mislabeled a jar. At seven, when he wound the tower mechanism, he turned the key too far and nearly cracked the spring.

All the while, he remembered Lena.

She had been seventeen when they discovered the hidden workshop. Elias’s father maintained the tower then, but he was not the Keeper; Mistress Ansel had chosen no apprentice. Elias and Lena, curious and foolish, had followed the old woman through the western stairwell and learned her secret.

Lena had not been afraid of the jars.

She had listened to them.

“This one contains a proposal someone never made,” she said, holding a pale blue bottle near her ear.

Mistress Ansel had caught them, of course. Elias expected fury. Instead, she had looked from him to Lena and said, “One of you may be taught. Time has opened the door for both, but it will close for one.”

Lena understood the jars instinctively. She could distinguish a wasted morning from a stolen afternoon by color alone. Elias needed weeks to learn what she grasped in minutes.

Yet Mistress Ansel chose Elias.

He never knew why.

For three years, Lena helped him study. They cleaned moonlight from the gears and trapped loose midnights before they escaped into dreams. They fell in love among the ticking clocks.

Then came the winter when Bellwether’s bells failed.

At 11:43 on the longest night of the year, the tower mechanism stopped.

Every clock in town stopped with it.

Mistress Ansel was away in the north, attending the funeral of another Keeper. Elias had been left in charge. He climbed into the mechanism and found a black shape wedged between the central gears.

A jar without a label.

It had cracked.

Darkness leaked from the fracture, swallowing seconds as it spread.

Lena found an old instruction in Mistress Ansel’s books: the damage could be repaired, but only if someone surrendered an unwounded hour—an hour of perfect happiness, freely given.

They had shared only one such hour.

It was a summer evening by the river, when swallows crossed a violet sky and Lena had promised to stay with him despite the strange duty he would inherit. They had lain in the grass until the stars appeared, saying nothing because nothing needed to be said.

Elias took that hour from Lena without telling her.

He knew how she loved the town. He knew she would sacrifice the memory willingly. But he also knew she might surrender another hour instead—one that did not contain him.

So, afraid of being erased, he chose for her.

He sealed the darkness with their summer evening.

The clocks began again.

Lena remembered the river and the swallows, but not the love she had felt. She remembered promising something, though not what. In the weeks that followed, she looked at Elias with increasing unease. She knew there was an absence inside her, and she knew he had made it.

When he confessed, she did not forgive him.

“I would have given the hour,” she said.

“I know.”

“But you wanted to choose what I lost.”

“Yes.”

“You call that love?”

He had no answer.

She left Bellwether soon after. Elias gave her the silver watch as a farewell gift, though neither of them said farewell properly.

Now she was dying.

At midnight, Elias stood before the black jars.

They occupied a locked cabinet at the back of the workshop. Most contained dangerous hours: moments in which time had been twisted by grief, violence, or impossible desire. Mistress Ansel had warned him never to open them. A returned happy hour might offer comfort. A returned black hour could change everything around it.

He unlocked the cabinet.

Inside were thirteen jars.

One held the last hour of a king who had tried to bargain with death. One contained a battlefield dawn that had occurred on three different days. Another held the memory of a child who had never been born.

On the lowest shelf rested the jar from that winter night.

Within its darkness glimmered a violet sky.

Elias lifted it out.

He could return Lena’s memory. The first rule forbade it, but rules were not walls. They were doors that responsible people agreed not to open.

He imagined visiting her bedside and placing the hour in her hands. She would remember the river, the swallows, and the promise. Perhaps she would understand him. Perhaps she would forgive him before the end.

Or perhaps he only wanted to choose for her again.

Elias sat on the floor until dawn.

At six, he swept the lost minutes into piles. There were more than usual. Across town, people had slept badly. In one corner he found forty-three minutes from a mother watching her daughter struggle to breathe. They were gray, almost black.

Lena’s minutes.

He placed them in a jar and did not label it.

At eight, the tower door opened without a knock.

Mara stood there, pale and furious.

“She asked for you again.”

Elias rose. “Who is with her?”

“No one. We have no one.”

“I’m sorry.”

“I don’t want you to be sorry. I want you to come.”

He looked around the workshop.

For eighteen years he had believed the tower would collapse without him. Perhaps that belief was another form of pride. Clocks had existed before Keepers. Time had existed before clocks.

He took his coat.

Mara’s anger faltered. “You’re coming?”

“Yes.”

They walked through Bellwether beneath a white autumn sky. Shops were opening around the square. Bakers arranged loaves behind windows. A postman cycled past with his satchel bouncing. None of them noticed the Keeper leaving his tower.

Mara and Lena lived above a closed bookshop on Candle Street. The apartment smelled of dust, rosemary, and medicine.

Lena lay near the window.

Her face was thinner than the one in Elias’s memory, but the years between vanished when she opened her eyes. They were the same gray-green eyes that had once reflected shelves of glowing time.

“You took long enough,” she whispered.

Elias tried to answer, but his voice failed.

Mara looked from one to the other. “I’ll make tea.”

“You hate making tea,” Lena said.

“I suddenly love it.”

She disappeared into the kitchen.

Elias sat beside the bed.

Lena studied him. “You got old.”

“So did you.”

“Not as much.”

“No. You were always better at everything.”

She smiled faintly. “Still feeling sorry for yourself?”

“Frequently.”

“Good. I’d hate to think you’d become unbearable.”

He looked at her hands. They were folded over the blanket, fragile as paper.

“I brought nothing,” he said.

“You came. That’s unusual enough.”

“Lena—”

“No. Don’t begin with an apology. We exhausted those years ago, even if you weren’t there for the conversation.”

He bowed his head.

After a while, she said, “I remember loving you.”

Elias looked up sharply.

“I don’t remember the hour you took,” she continued. “But I remember the shape around it. People think forgetting is emptiness. It isn’t. An absence has edges. I spent years touching them.”

“I can give it back.”

Her eyes moved to his coat pocket.

He had not brought the black jar. Yet for one terrible moment he wondered if she could see it in the tower, waiting in darkness.

“You kept it,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Of course you did.”

“I thought you might want it.”

“No. You thought you might want me to have it.”

The truth landed gently because it had landed before.

Elias nodded.

Lena turned toward the window. Across the street, a row of clocks stood in a watchmaker’s display. Each showed a slightly different time.

“Do you know why Ansel chose you?” she asked.

“No.”

“I asked her once.”

His breath caught. “What did she say?”

“She said I loved time for what it gave people. You feared it for what it took away.”

“That sounds like a reason to choose you.”

“It was. But Ansel knew I would break every rule the first time someone begged me. She knew you would keep them.”

“I nearly opened the jar last night.”

“But you didn’t.”

“No.”

Lena smiled. “Infuriating woman. Still right after all these years.”

Mara returned with three cups. The tea was much too strong, and Elias drank it gratefully.

For several hours, they talked.

Lena told him about the life she had built beyond Bellwether. She had married a musician named Tomas Quill, who died when Mara was six. She had restored old books, traveled through coastal villages, and once spent a winter living in a lighthouse. She had returned to Bellwether two years ago because, she claimed, every sensible person eventually returned to argue with the place that made them.

Mara asked questions when the silence became dangerous.

“Did my mother really climb the tower during storms?”

“Yes.”

“Did she really fix the clock using a hairpin?”

“Twice.”

“Did she push you off the roof?”

“Only onto a lower roof.”

“He deserved it,” Lena said.

“I assumed so.”

By evening, her voice had weakened. Mara helped her drink water. Elias watched the window darken and heard clocks chiming across town.

Not one agreed with another.

He felt each lost second like a tug behind his ribs. The workshop would be filling. Minutes would gather beneath the shelves. Unsorted hours might bleed into one another.

Still he remained.

At ten, Lena began drifting in and out of sleep.

At eleven, she opened her eyes and gripped Elias’s wrist.

“The bells,” she said.

“What about them?”

“They’re going to fail.”

Above the rooftops, the tower clock struck the quarter hour.

“You’re dreaming,” Mara whispered.

Lena stared at Elias. “11:43.”

Cold moved through him.

The silver watch lay on the bedside table. Its hands, motionless for fifteen years, trembled.

Then they began to move.

11:41.

11:42.

Elias stood so quickly that his chair fell backward.

“What’s happening?” Mara asked.

The watch clicked.

11:43.

Every clock in Bellwether stopped.

Silence struck the town.

Not ordinary silence, but the deep, suspended quiet of a world between heartbeats. Outside the window, a moth hung motionless above a lamp. Rain froze against the glass. Mara stood beside the bed without blinking.

Only Elias and Lena could move.

“Why?” Elias whispered.

Lena’s grip tightened. “The hour wants to return.”

In his mind, he saw the black jar in the tower. The darkness inside had waited fifteen years, and now, as Lena approached death, the stolen hour was pulling toward its owner.

“The seal is breaking,” he said.

“What happens if it breaks?”

“Everything trapped with the hour will be released.”

“The darkness?”

“Yes.”

“And the town?”

“Time may turn backward. Or repeat. Or stop permanently.”

Lena laughed weakly. “You Keepers have wonderfully precise answers.”

“I have to go.”

“You won’t reach the tower. Not between seconds.”

She was right. The town lay frozen because there was no time in which to cross it.

Elias looked at the silver watch. A faint violet glow escaped its seams.

“The watch is connected to the jar,” he said. “It remembers the same hour.”

“Then use it.”

“To do what?”

“Open the hour here.”

“That could kill you.”

“I am dying, Elias.”

“It could erase everything that came after. Your marriage. Mara.”

“Then don’t give the hour back to me.”

The watch glowed brighter.

The room changed.

Summer grass spread across the floorboards. The walls dissolved into a violet sky. Swallows wheeled above the bed, and the scent of the river filled the air.

Elias saw two figures lying beneath an alder tree: himself at twenty, Lena beside him. Their hands almost touched in the grass.

The lost hour had returned, but it remained unfinished, waiting for a choice.

Elias understood.

The seal required an hour of perfect happiness. He had used Lena’s half, but not his own. He had kept his memory, treasured it, revisited it in dreams. That imbalance had cracked the seal from within.

He had taken from her what he had refused to surrender himself.

“I know how to repair it,” he said.

Lena followed his gaze to their younger selves. “Your memory.”

“Yes.”

“If you give it up, you won’t remember loving me.”

“I’ll remember the shape around it.”

Tears brightened her eyes.

Elias reached toward the vision.

Lena caught his hand. “Wait.”

The swallows paused overhead.

“All these years,” she said, “I thought I wanted you to understand exactly what you took from me. I wanted justice so much that I polished it into cruelty.”

“You were right.”

“I was hurt. That isn’t always the same thing.”

The younger Lena laughed beneath the alder tree, though no sound came. Elias could not remember what had amused her. He had believed the memory perfect, but already parts were missing.

Time took everything eventually.

The cruelty lay in pretending otherwise.

“I’m afraid,” he said.

“I know.”

“Will you forgive me?”

Lena looked toward Mara, frozen beside the bed with one hand around a cup of bitter tea.

“I forgave you years ago,” she said. “I was waiting for you to forgive the world for continuing.”

Elias closed his eyes and placed both hands around the watch.

The summer hour opened.

Warmth moved through him: river wind, crushed grass, Lena’s shoulder against his, the first evening star. He felt the absolute certainty of being young and loved. For one final instant, he held the whole hour.

Then he let it go.

The memory flowed into the watch like light into a well.

The violet sky faded. The swallows became shadows, then vanished. Floorboards returned beneath his knees.

Across Bellwether, the clocks began again.

Rain struck the window. The moth flew into the dark. Mara dropped her cup, and it shattered.

Lena released a long breath.

Elias knew he had lost something, but he did not know what.

He was kneeling beside a dying woman whose hand he held with great tenderness. He remembered meeting her in the tower as a girl. He remembered their studies, their quarrel, and her departure. But the center of those memories was quiet and bright-edged, like a missing pane in a stained-glass window.

“Did it work?” Mara asked.

“Yes,” Elias said.

Lena looked at him.

“Do you know me?” she whispered.

He touched the swallow engraved on the watch.

“I know the shape of you.”

She smiled.

Shortly before dawn, Lena Quill died while the clocks of Bellwether kept imperfect time.

After the funeral, Elias returned to the tower.

The workshop was a disaster. Lost minutes covered the floor in drifts. Jars had overflowed. A full Tuesday afternoon had escaped and hidden behind the furnace. He spent three days restoring order.

Mara arrived on the fourth morning.

She wore her mother’s green coat and carried two cups of tea.

“I don’t need an apprentice,” Elias said.

“I didn’t ask.”

“You used the secret knock.”

“I like the secret knock.”

“You can’t stay.”

She stepped past him and surveyed the shelves. “That jar is mislabeled.”

“It is not.”

“It says SLEEPLESS NIGHTS, but the light is blue. Sleepless nights are gray.”

“Usually.”

She lifted the jar and listened. “This is waiting. Someone spent these hours waiting.”

Elias frowned and took it from her. The light inside pulsed with the dull rhythm of a railway station clock.

He fetched a new label.

“You can stay until noon,” he said.

Mara smiled in precisely the way someone else once had, though Elias could not remember when.

Years later, when Elias finally left the tower, the shelves were orderly, the gears shone, and Bellwether’s clocks were losing only the proper amount of time.

Mara became the next Keeper.

Unlike Elias, she was not afraid of what time took. Unlike her mother, she did not believe every loss should be undone. She understood that an absence could wound, but it could also shape the life that grew around it.

She kept the silver watch on her workbench.

Its hands never moved again.

On certain summer evenings, however, when swallows crossed the violet sky, the watch grew warm. Mara would open its lid and hear two young people laughing beside a river.

She never saw their faces.

She never opened the black jar that held their hour.

But she added a new rule beneath the three Mistress Ansel had written long before:

WHAT IS LOST IS NOT ALWAYS GONE.

Then she would climb the western stairs, open the tower windows, and let the bells ring over Bellwether, carrying the present moment outward—bright, brief, and enough.
